unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 10 gathers the whole of Grade 8 into one evidence-led capstone. You revise thirty review words drawn from Units 1 to 8, from concise, zeal and articulate to benign, disposition and clarify. Six grammar workshops bring back comparatives and superlatives, the passive voice in four tenses, the past perfect and present perfect continuous, reported speech, conditionals, and the phrasal verbs, reflexive pronouns and quantifiers that polish a final draft. Five review texts revisit the year's stories, from Whispers Beyond the Gate to The Curtain Never Lies. You then build an inquiry product for a defined audience, defend it aloud for five to six minutes and reflect on the reader, writer and speaker you have become.
unit.learningPath: Revisit the thirty review words. Reread five review texts drawn from Units 1 to 9. Rebuild the year's grammar in six editing workshops. Curate and annotate portfolio evidence. Draft, revise and polish the evidence-led inquiry product. Rehearse and deliver the six-minute defence. Reflect toward Grade 9 and complete the final course quiz.
howToUse: This is your capstone: one project that draws on the whole year. There is no video — start by reading the project page.
The five readings are review texts, each drawing on two units from the year. Reread them and answer the comprehension checks.
Writing and Speaking are one inquiry: annotate your portfolio evidence, write the proposal, draft from evidence, revise from feedback, then rehearse and deliver the six-minute defence.
The Final course quiz is on this page, after every section has a tick. It is extra — it does not lock the unit.

readings.title: Review text 1: Whispers, Signals and the Truth Test (Units 1 and 2)
readings.setting: The harbour city and Horizon Youth Radio, revisited for the capstone
readings.passageScript:
How quickly can a whisper cross a city? Unit 1 opened your Grade 8 year with that uncomfortable question, and its answer has shadowed every unit since. In 'The Speed of a Whisper' you learnt that a rumour travels fastest when it flatters our fears, because frightened readers share first and check later. The companion text, 'The Fact-Checker's Toolkit', handed you four steady questions to slow that race: who wrote this, when was it written, what evidence supports it, and who benefits if I believe it? Those questions looked simple in September. By June you knew they were the difference between an informed reader and a gullible one.

The story 'Whispers Beyond the Gate' turned the lesson into drama. Amal noticed the hoax flyer on a temperate harbour morning, long before the crowds gathered on Harbour Road. She and Nora told themselves they were only going to observe the protest, yet the noise nearly swallowed them both. What saved them was not luck but a stubborn zeal for the truth. Amal underlined one warning in her notebook: if we let rumours think for us, someone else will think for us. When the two friends launched their questioning club, forty students arrived at the first meeting, some nervous, some angry, all curious. Their rule was concise: if you cannot cite a source, you cannot repeat the claim. Whereas the flyer had built a barricade of fear between neighbours, the club dismantled that barricade question by question.

Unit 2 widened the lens from words to design. 'Packaging the Truth' showed how a bold font, a calm colour and a tidy layout can make a weak claim feel plausible before a single sentence has been read. Honest designers match the promise on the box to the product inside it; careless ones let the wrapping usurp the message. The unit tied design to sustainability as well, arguing that a message, like a package, should be built to last and honest to recycle. Claims with real longevity are the ones that still hold true a year after the poster fades.

The story 'Signal in the Static' gave those ideas a newsroom. Imani and Kofi run Horizon Youth Radio, a student station whose motto promises news and truth from the city's students, for the city's future. An anonymous tip pointed them toward a secret land deal that threatened the community gardens, so the pair had to decipher documents, verify names and weigh every risk aloud. When a masked caller warned them to stop pushing and hinted they would forfeit more than files, they refused to feign ignorance. They checked the evidence again, invited the officials to respond, and broadcast only what they could prove. The applause afterwards came from not everyone, but enough, and the two presenters felt steady rather than triumphant. That steadiness, the story suggests, is what earned joy feels like.

Read side by side, the two units share one engine: reported speech. Amal reported that the flyer's author had never been found. Kofi admitted that the investigation frightened him, yet argued that stopping would cost the gardens far more. Notice how the tense steps back and the pronouns swap whenever speech is reported; that small grammar carries the whole discipline of quoting people fairly. As you assemble your capstone inquiry, treat these units as your standards office. Every claim deserves the toolkit's four questions, every quotation deserves honest reporting, and every design choice should serve the message it carries, never disguise it.

readings.title: Review text 2: Voices That Move a Community (Units 3 and 4)
readings.theme: Community action, advertising and honest persuasion
readings.setting: Kilimo Bay and a Mogadishu technology academy, revisited for the capstone
readings.passageScript:
Unit 3 began with a hard look at a beautiful place. In the story 'Rising Tide', Kilimo Bay had once been clear and full of fish, but debris now danced on the waves: torn fishing nets, plastic wrappers, even a cracked sandal. The story's young founder refused to look away from the water she loved. She gathered friends into a movement called Coastal Rise, and within a month the change was visible along the whole shoreline. New bins were being affixed along the beach paths, school clubs were hosting weekend clean-ups, and elders were telling bonfire stories about the bay's older, cleaner days. The information text 'When a Community Decides to Act' explained why such movements succeed: they start small, they stay visible, and they hand every neighbour a job worth doing. The unit also trained your formal voice. You practised openings such as 'It is imperative that the council acts now', because officials listen hardest when a serious request arrives in serious clothes. When the founder finally addressed the town, her speech ended a sentence with a preposition on purpose, the way confident speakers do. The applause rolled from the back rows to the front like a wave coming home.

Unit 4 crossed from persuasion for a cause to persuasion for profit. 'The Power of Persuasion' named the techniques that advertisers aim at you every day. Emotional appeals tug before you think, bandwagon pressure whispers that everyone else has one, and glittering promises sparkle while proving nothing. The story 'Code Name: Bonanza' staged the contest in the open. At a technology academy in Mogadishu, student teams entered the Innovation for Impact challenge, and the final filled the auditorium with parents, reporters and school heads. Nadir of Team Horizon delivered the slickest pitch of the day, promising that his product, The Beacon, would transform waste into wealth. His smile was wide, his tone polished, his evidence thin. The winning team answered differently. They had rehearsed until their answers felt natural, trained themselves to speak with calm authority, and brought working results instead of dazzling claims. One inventor's hands still smelled faintly of soldering metal on the final morning. The judges' verdict carried the story's quiet lesson. A cunning adversary can bend an audience's attention for ten minutes, but momentum built on honest work is far harder to stop. Winning with integrity, the story insists, is still winning.

The grammar of these units matched their arguments. The second conditional let you test imagined worlds and judge the real one against them. If every advert were honest, persuasion would be a public service; if the bay were left alone, the debris would win. Verbs and adjectives kept their partner prepositions, so volunteers were proud of their beaches and worried about their harvests, never proud about them. Reflexive pronouns reminded speakers that the first audience they must convince is themselves.

Hold the two units together and one truth emerges: voices move communities when evidence walks beside emotion. Coastal Rise won its neighbours with visible results, not with slogans painted twice as large. The academy judges rewarded proof over polish. Your capstone product will face the same examiners in miniature, so borrow both playbooks. Speak with the warmth of a volunteer, argue with the precision of an engineer, and let no deceptive shortcut, however tempting, into work that carries your name.

readings.title: Review text 3: The Sea, the Highlands and Their Keepers (Units 5 and 6)
readings.theme: Natural resources, conservation and patient responsibility
readings.setting: The town of Marka and the Simien Highlands, revisited for the capstone
readings.passageScript:
Unit 5 sailed to Marka, a shoreline town that looked pristine at first glance. Tariq knew better than to trust a first glance. Plastic bottles hung in old fishing nets near the ancient coral rocks, sweet wrappers drifted with the current, and the calm surface proved deceptive in the way calm surfaces often are. He and Amara refused to be naive about what they saw. Instead of complaining, they counted. For weeks they gathered samples, recorded numbers and turned observations into charts, exactly as the information text 'How Scientists Read a Coastline' recommends. When doubters asked why anyone should listen to students, Amara's answer was simple: show them everything — the charts, the samples, the counts, all of it. Posters went up in every street, flyers changed hands at the Friday market, and the town meeting overflowed. The mayor made a promise worth quoting: 'The first units will be installed by December.' Amara reported that the council had confirmed the timeline, and the transition to cleaner water management began. The story 'Shifting Currents' closes with quiet rewards rather than fireworks. Amara was invited to join the national youth council for environmental leadership, and Tariq began an internship at a marine research centre. Their grandfather walked the shore with Tariq again, just as they had done years before.

Unit 6 climbed from the coast into the Simien Highlands, where a school expedition followed a twisting trail toward the stone fortress locals call the Citadel of Wind and Stone. Their destination stood on a ridge like a crown, and the mountain tested judgement long before it tested legs. One team member slipped away to climb alone, hungry for the glory of arriving first. Wind pushed against the walls hard enough to deter even the strongest from rushing. Zara, the group's leader, chose the long, safer route and refused to let pride split the team apart. The story's verdict is a quiet conditional: if the lone climber had reached the citadel first, he might have claimed victory, but he would have learned nothing. The unit's information texts asked the harder public questions. 'The Roof of Africa' celebrated wonders worth keeping. 'Should the High Trails Close?' set two honest voices against each other: a guide who feeds his family from tourism and a scientist counting damaged slopes. The park wardens hoped the new signs would deter visitors from leaving the marked trails. Conservation, the unit argued, is rarely one dramatic rescue; it is a thousand small refusals to do harm.

Grammar grew out of both landscapes. The future passive carried official promises, since pipes will be laid and trails will be repaired by people who must then be held to it. Comparatives and superlatives measured the highlands honestly: the final climb was steeper than the morning trail, and the ridge path was the most exposed of all. Quantifiers portioned out scarce resources — a few litres of clean water, plenty of patience, most of the work still ahead.

When your capstone defends a recommendation, remember Marka and the mountains together. Bring counts rather than impressions, because the sea rewarded the students who measured it. Compare fairly, because the mountain punished the climber who raced it. And when a striking view or a striking claim tempts you to rush, let the evidence set your pace so you never falter on the facts.

readings.title: Review text 4: Legacies Written in Ink and Voice (Units 7 and 8)
readings.theme: Historical legacy and the power of storytelling
readings.setting: Kambazi School in 1948 and the Dar es Salaam StoryForge, revisited for the capstone
readings.passageScript:
What survives of a person after the noise of their lifetime fades? Unit 7 answered with history, Unit 8 with art, and the pair became the heart of the year for many readers.

'The Rebellion of Silence' took you to Kambazi School in 1948, where stone paths twisted between mango trees and the dormitory walls wore their age openly. Among the Form 4 students was Jamal, quiet in the classroom and unshakeable outside it. When the school banned debate, most students obeyed and a few grumbled. Jamal did neither. His anonymous essays, printed by hand and passed under desks, said calmly what the ban had tried to bury. His essays could articulate what other students only felt. Two days after the first essay appeared, another arrived, written by someone else entirely; then another, and another, until a patient, systematic network had formed. The headmaster's dining-hall speech seemed benign on its surface, all warm concern for studies and futures. Yet it offered the writers no real reprieve, only a politer version of the same silence. The information text 'Legacy: The People History Remembers' supplied the unit's measuring stick: history keeps the names of people who changed what others could say, think or become. Decades later, an older Jamal told his interviewer that silence was safe, but safety is not the same as freedom, and freedom does not always shout. Sometimes it waits, listens and then speaks.

Unit 8 carried that idea onto a stage. Every year the coastal city of Dar es Salaam teems with talent during the National Youth StoryForge, but this year the rules had changed. For the first time, judges asked not only how a story sounded but what it did for the people listening. Imani entered as a storyteller with an uncanny gift and a private fear that her words might vanish the moment she spoke them. Her line about the boats engrossed the hall so completely that Tia, a rival finalist, admitted she had stopped breathing. Finals week assailed everyone; one student fainted, two withdrew, and Imani herself needed a night to recuperate before the last round. She steadied her disposition, spoke to serve rather than to perform, and discovered that stories are not fragile at all. Words, the story promises, waft into corners their speaker will never see. 'Why Stories Shape the World' made the same case in plain prose: stories preserve memories, carry values across borders, and give a voice to communities that ledgers and headlines forget. The unit's close reading, 'The Grammar of a Good Story', then opened the machinery behind the magic, from patient pacing to precise, load-bearing verbs.

The grammar of both units was the grammar of time. The past perfect ordered history's layers, because by the time the headmaster spoke, the network of writers had already formed. The present perfect continuous measured effort still warm: Imani has been shaping her closing story since the opening round. Reported speech turned testimony into record, letting one generation quote another without a defect creeping into the meaning.

For your capstone, these units set the standard of seriousness. Ask what your inquiry leaves behind. A finished product is pleasant; a legacy, however small, is better. Write so that a reader you will never meet could pick up your work, understand its evidence, and feel that someone had told them the truth with both ink and voice.

readings.title: Review text 5: The Curtain, the Chorus and the Road Ahead (Unit 9 and the Year in Review)
readings.theme: Performance, universal language and the Grade 8 capstone
readings.setting: Kampala's Youth Performing Arts Centre and the Grade 8 classroom, closing the year
readings.passageScript:
Unit 9 ended the year under stage lights. Kampala's Youth Performing Arts Centre pulsed with anticipation on the night of the regional finals, its chandeliers shaped like butterflies and its seats filling with schools from across East Africa. Backstage, disaster arrived on schedule: the production's centrepiece mask had vanished from the dressing room. Suspicion fell instantly on the rival team, whose leader later smirked and asked whether anyone could prove it. Rohan, the young director at the centre of 'The Curtain Never Lies', gave the answer the whole year had been teaching. No, he could not prove it, so he would not accuse; he named the behaviour repugnant and walked back to his cast. They rewrote the scene, performed without the mask, and collapsed into laughter and relief when the curtain fell. When the mask mysteriously reappeared in the final scene of their second performance, the crowd gasped as though a ghost had returned, and someone whispered what a story, what a choice. Two festival coordinators, one from Johannesburg and one from Nairobi, approached the cast before the week ended. Asked what young artists should remember, Rohan answered with the line this course would happily print on its cover. Do not just ask what you want to say; ask what your story does to people.

The unit's information text argued that music deserves its title of universal language because melody carries feeling across borders that vocabulary cannot cross. A song can hand you joy or sorrow in a language you have never studied. Performance, in other words, is communication with the packaging removed, and after a year of studying packaging, you were ready to hear that. The close reading 'Behind the Curtain' made the same case from backstage, where every effect an audience feels has been planned twice.

Now stand back and look at the whole road. You began among whispers in a harbour city, learning with Amal and Nora to question before repeating. You watched student journalists broadcast only what they could prove, and young organisers turn a polluted bay into a community's shared project, one weekend clean-up at a time. You weighed slick pitches against soldered evidence in Mogadishu, read a coastline like a scientist in Marka, and climbed toward a citadel that rewarded patience over pride. You met a quiet essayist whose hidden ink outlived a ban, a storyteller whose words wafted further than her fear, and a director who refused to accuse without proof. Nine units, nine settings, one steady lesson: language is power, and power demands evidence, fairness and craft.

The capstone asks you to prove you own that lesson. Over the coming weeks you will curate your strongest work, frame an inquiry question that matters to a real audience. You will verify your sources with the Unit 1 toolkit, then draft, revise and polish an evidence-led product. Teacher Yasmin will conference with you at every milestone, but the choices belong to you now. The final act is a five- to six-minute spoken defence, followed by questions you cannot fully predict, which is precisely why it counts. Rehearse until your comparatives are fair, your passives deliberate, your reported speech accurate and your conditionals honest.

When the curtain rises on your defence, remember Rohan's rule and turn it on yourself. Do not only ask what you want to say about your year. Ask what your evidence does to the people listening, and make sure the answer is: it convinces them.

comprehension.explanation: A main-idea retrieval: the four toolkit questions are listed in the opening paragraph of the review text.

comprehension.question: What evidence does Review text 1 give that the Horizon Youth Radio investigation carried real risk for Imani and Kofi?

comprehension.explanation: An evidence question: the threat and the pair's response sit in the Signal in the Static paragraph.

comprehension.question: What does Review text 2 say made Coastal Rise succeed where louder appeals might have failed?

comprehension.explanation: A synthesis main-idea question answered by the closing paragraph, which joins the two settings deliberately.

comprehension.question: What proof did Tariq and Amara bring to the Marka town meeting, and what promise did it win?

comprehension.explanation: An evidence-retrieval question: both the data list and the mayor's quoted promise appear in the Unit 5 paragraph.

comprehension.question: According to Review text 4, what standard does 'Legacy: The People History Remembers' use to decide who history keeps?
comprehension.correctAnswer: History keeps the names of people who changed what others could say, think or become, like Jamal and his hidden essay network.
comprehension.explanation: A main-idea question: the measuring-stick sentence sits at the centre of the Unit 7 paragraph.

comprehension.correctAnswer: He admitted he could not prove it, so he refused to accuse anyone; he called the behaviour repugnant and led his cast to rewrite and perform without the mask.
comprehension.explanation: An evidence question about the backstage confrontation and the cast's response in the Unit 9 retelling.

comprehension.correctAnswer: If you cannot cite a source, you cannot repeat the claim; the rule dismantled the barricade of fear the hoax flyer had built between neighbours.
comprehension.explanation: A main-idea question about the club's founding rule in the Whispers Beyond the Gate paragraph.

comprehension.correctAnswer: They hoped the signs would deter visitors from leaving the marked trails, protecting slopes already counted as damaged.
comprehension.explanation: An evidence question answered by the conservation debate sentences in the Unit 6 paragraph.

grammar.title: Comparatives, superlatives and comparative adverbs (Units 2, 6 and 8)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: You compared designs in Unit 2, mountains in Unit 6 and performances in Unit 8, and the same machinery drove all three. Comparatives weigh two things against each other; superlatives crown one out of three or more; comparative adverbs compare how actions are done. Your capstone will compare sources, viewpoints and drafts, so this is the grammar your conclusions will stand on.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Short adjectives take -er and -est: the final climb was steeper than the morning trail, and the ridge path was the steepest stretch of all. Longer adjectives take more and most: Nadir's pitch was more polished, but the winning pitch was the most convincing of the day. Watch the spelling changes: big, bigger; early, earlier; simple, simpler. Irregulars must be memorised: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further, furthest. Adverbs compare actions: Zara climbed more carefully than the lone climber, and Rohan spoke more calmly than his rival. Use as ... as for equality: no advert is as persuasive as working proof.
grammar.commonMistake: Stacking both markers at once -- 'more steeper', 'most steepest' -- or crowning a superlative when only two things are compared. If your inquiry weighs two sources, the stronger one is 'the more reliable of the two', never 'the most reliable'.
grammar.memoryTip: Two things? Reach for -er or more. Three or more? Take the -est or the most. Never wear both badges on one word.
grammar.practice: Part A — choose the correct form: 1) Of the two pitches, Nadir's was (slicker / the slickest). 2) The citadel route was the (more exposed / most exposed) of the three trails. 3) Imani told her story (more quietly / most quietly) than the other finalists. 4) The bay looked (cleaner / more clean) after every weekend clean-up. 5) Of all nine units, which reading did you find (harder / the hardest)? Part B — write three fair comparisons for your capstone: compare two of your sources, two of your drafts, and two review texts, using one comparative adjective, one superlative and one comparative adverb. Answer key: Part A — 1) slicker (only two pitches are compared, so the comparative wins, not the superlative). 2) the most exposed (three trails are compared, so the superlative is required). 3) more quietly ("than the other finalists" signals a comparison, so the comparative adverb form is correct). 4) cleaner ("clean" is a short adjective, so it takes -er; "more clean" is never correct). 5) the hardest ("of all nine units" signals more than two, so the superlative is required). Part B asks you to write your own comparisons about your sources, drafts and review texts, so there is no fixed line to check — as a self-check, confirm you used exactly one comparative adjective (such as -er or more + adjective), one superlative (such as -est or most + adjective, comparing three or more items) and one comparative adverb (such as more carefully), and that no sentence stacks two markers on one word (as in "more steeper").

grammar.title: The passive voice across the year: present, past, continuous and future (Units 2, 3, 4 and 5)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: The passive keeps the spotlight on what was done when the doer matters less, which is why reports, notices and official promises lean on it. You met it in four costumes this year: the simple present and past in Units 2 and 4, the present continuous passive in Unit 3, and the future passive in Unit 5. Your capstone's method section will need at least two of them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Build every passive from be plus a past participle, and let the tense live in 'be'. Present simple: the winning entries are judged on evidence. Past simple: the hoax flyer was printed on cheap paper. Present continuous: new bins are being affixed along the beach paths. Future: the first units will be installed by December. Add the doer with 'by' only when it earns its place: the land deal was uncovered by two student journalists. If the doer is obvious or unknown, leave it out and let the action speak.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping 'be' from the future passive -- 'the units will installed' -- or flooding a whole paragraph with passives until nobody in it seems to do anything. Choose the passive deliberately, sentence by sentence, and keep your strongest claims active.
grammar.memoryTip: Passive equals be plus past participle; the tense hides inside 'be'. Find the doer, and if the deed matters more, promote the deed.
grammar.practice: Part A — turn each active sentence into the passive, keeping the tense: 1) Volunteers are cleaning the bay every weekend. 2) The council confirmed the timeline. 3) Judges will announce the winners on Friday. 4) The academy displays the winning inventions. Part B — name the passive tense in each: 1) The trails are being repaired this month. 2) The essays were passed under desks. 3) The results will be published by the ministry. Part C — find one sentence in your capstone draft that would be stronger in the passive, rewrite it, and note why the doer could step aside. Answer key: Part A — 1) The bay is being cleaned every weekend (by volunteers) — present continuous passive. 2) The timeline was confirmed (by the council) — past simple passive. 3) The winners will be announced on Friday (by the judges) — future passive. 4) The winning inventions are displayed (by the academy) — present simple passive. Part B — 1) present continuous passive. 2) past simple passive. 3) future passive. Part C asks you to find and rewrite a sentence from your own capstone draft, so there is no fixed line to check — as a self-check, confirm your rewritten sentence uses a form of "be" plus a past participle, keeps the original tense, and only adds "by" if naming the doer genuinely earns its place.

grammar.title: Past perfect and present perfect continuous (Units 7, 8 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Two tenses ordered time for you this year. The past perfect reaches further back from a past moment, so history keeps its layers straight: by the time the headmaster spoke, the essay network had already formed. The present perfect continuous measures effort still warm and unfinished: Imani has been shaping her story since the opening round. Your reflection will need both, because Grade 8 is now a past with layers of its own.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Past perfect: had plus past participle, for the earlier of two past events. Jamal had written three essays before the ban was even announced. By the finals, two contestants had withdrawn. Present perfect continuous: has or have been plus the -ing form, for duration up to now. Rohan has been directing his own play for over a year. We have been revising the passive since Tuesday. Signal words help: 'by the time', 'already' and 'before' often call the past perfect, while 'since', 'for' and 'how long' invite the continuous.
grammar.commonMistake: Sprinkling the past perfect over every past sentence to sound formal. It only earns its keep when two past times need ordering; a simple story told in sequence stays in the past simple.
grammar.memoryTip: Had happened first; has been happening still. One tense looks over its shoulder, the other checks its watch.
grammar.practice: Part A — put the verb in the past perfect or past simple: 1) By the time the curtain rose, the cast ______ (rewrite) the scene twice. 2) The judges ______ (announce) the theme before the teams arrived. 3) When Amal reached Harbour Road, the crowd ______ (gather) already. Part B — put the verb in the present perfect continuous: 1) I ______ (prepare) my defence since Monday. 2) How long ______ you ______ (work) on your inquiry question? 3) She ______ (collect) sources for three weeks. Part C — write two sentences about your own year, one with each tense, and check the time words justify your choice. Answer key: Part A — 1) had rewritten (past perfect: the rewriting happened before the curtain rose). 2) had announced (past perfect: the announcement came before the teams arrived). 3) had gathered (past perfect, signalled by "already": the gathering was complete before Amal reached Harbour Road). Part B — 1) have been preparing. 2) have you been working. 3) has been collecting. Part C asks you to write two sentences about your own year, so there is no fixed line to check — as a self-check, confirm your past-perfect sentence names two past events in the correct order (the earlier one in the past perfect) and your present perfect continuous sentence includes a duration word such as "since" or "for" that justifies the tense.

grammar.title: Reported speech: statements, questions and commands (Units 1, 5, 7, 8 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Reported speech appeared in five of your nine units because every one of their stories turned on testimony: what the caller warned, what the mayor promised, what the headmaster demanded. Reporting speech fairly means stepping the tense back, swapping the pointers, and keeping the speaker's meaning without stealing their words. Your capstone's source record depends on doing this cleanly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Statements step one tense back and shift pronouns and time words: the mayor said, 'The first units will be installed by December' becomes the mayor said that the first units would be installed by December. Questions lose their question order and their question mark: 'Where is the studio?' becomes she asked where the studio was; yes-or-no questions take whether or if. Commands take told plus object plus to-infinitive: the headmaster told the students to focus on their books; negatives add not, as in he warned them not to stop verifying.
grammar.commonMistake: Keeping question word order inside a reported question -- 'she asked where was the studio' -- or leaving now, here and tomorrow unshifted so the report contradicts its own timeline. Step the pointers back with the tense: now becomes then, here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day.
grammar.memoryTip: Report in three moves: tense back one step, pointers pushed away, question order flattened. Say the original aloud, then retell it to someone who was not there.
grammar.practice: Part A — report each statement: 1) Kofi said, 'The documents are genuine.' 2) Amara announced, 'The council has confirmed the timeline.' 3) The caller warned, 'You will forfeit more than files.' Part B — report each question: 1) 'Where did the flyer come from?' Nora asked. 2) 'Can you prove it?' the rival leader asked. Part C — report each command: 1) 'Bring the charts to the meeting,' Tariq told the volunteers. 2) 'Do not accuse anyone without proof,' Rohan told the cast. Then reread Part C and circle every pointer you shifted. Answer key: Part A — 1) Kofi said (that) the documents were genuine. 2) Amara announced that the council had confirmed the timeline. 3) The caller warned that [the listener] would forfeit more than files (the pronoun "you" shifts to whichever pronoun matches the person actually warned — "he", "she" or "they" — since the report is no longer spoken straight to that person). Part B — 1) Nora asked where the flyer had come from. 2) The rival leader asked if/whether [the listener] could prove it. Part C — 1) Tariq told the volunteers to bring the charts to the meeting. 2) Rohan told the cast not to accuse anyone without proof. Rereading Part C: neither command actually contains a pointer word such as "now", "here" or "tomorrow", so there is nothing to circle in these two — the only change each makes is trading the imperative for "told + object + to-infinitive" (adding "not" before the infinitive for the negative).

grammar.title: Conditionals: zero, first and second (Units 1, 2, 3 and 4)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Conditionals let your writing test the world before acting in it. The zero conditional states what is always true, the first weighs a real tomorrow, and the second imagines a present that is not the case. Across Units 1 to 4 they powered fact-checking rules, newsroom decisions and community appeals, and your capstone recommendation will almost certainly end in one.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Zero conditional, for general truths: if a rumour flatters its reader, it spreads faster. First conditional, for real possibilities: if we verify the documents, we will broadcast the story; unless the council acts, the gardens will be lost. Second conditional, for imagined situations now: if the bay were cleaner, more fish would return; if every advert were honest, persuasion would be a public service. Note the pattern of each: zero takes present plus present, first takes present plus will, second takes past plus would, and careful writers prefer 'were' over 'was' after if.
grammar.commonMistake: Letting 'would' invade the if-clause: 'if the bay would be cleaner' promises nothing and means less. Keep would in the result half of the sentence, and keep will out of the if-clause entirely.
grammar.memoryTip: Zero is always, first is likely, second is imaginary. If the if-clause contains would or will, the sentence has sprung a leak.
grammar.practice: Part A — name the conditional and finish the sentence sensibly: 1) If a claim has no source, ... 2) If we publish tonight, ... 3) If every town had a Coastal Rise club, ... Part B — correct the faulty conditionals: 1) If the trails would close, the guides will lose work. 2) Unless we will hurry, the meeting starts without us. Part C — write the closing recommendation of your capstone twice, once as a first conditional for your realistic proposal and once as a second conditional for your ambitious one, then decide which your evidence supports. Answer key: Part A names the conditional and invites your own sensible ending, so treat these as models rather than the only correct wording — 1) zero conditional, a general truth: if a claim has no source, it loses credibility. 2) first conditional, a real possibility: if we publish tonight, we will reach readers before the story changes. 3) second conditional, an imagined present: if every town had a Coastal Rise club, more neighbourhoods would organise the same way. As a self-check, confirm your own completions keep the pattern for their type: present plus present for zero, present plus will for first, past plus would for second. Part B — 1) If the trails close, the guides will lose work (remove "would" from the if-clause; the first conditional keeps will only in the result). 2) Unless we hurry, the meeting will start without us (remove "will" from the unless-clause and add it to the result instead). Part C asks you to write your own capstone recommendation twice, so there is no fixed line to check — as a self-check, confirm your first-conditional version uses present plus will and your second-conditional version uses past plus would, with will or would never appearing inside an if-clause or unless-clause.

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs, reflexive pronouns and quantifiers: the final edit (Units 1, 4, 6, 7 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Three smaller systems give Grade 8 writing its natural stride, and this last workshop gathers them for your final edit. Phrasal verbs carry everyday precision, reflexive pronouns point actions back at their doers, and quantifiers measure nouns honestly. Editors check all three in a single pass, and so will you.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Phrasal verbs pair a verb with a particle that changes its meaning: the expedition set off at dawn; the officials tried to play down the report; the journalists promised to look into the deal; nobody gave up. Reflexive pronouns mirror the subject: Imani reminded herself to breathe; the team trained themselves to answer calmly; I timed myself twice. Quantifiers fit the noun they measure: a few sources, a little time, plenty of patience, most of the work, each milestone. Countable nouns take few and many; uncountable nouns take little and much.
grammar.commonMistake: Inventing reflexives that do not exist -- 'hisself' and 'theirselves' are never correct; the forms are himself and themselves. With quantifiers, watch the countable line: 'less sources' should be fewer sources, though less time is right because time is uncountable.
grammar.memoryTip: Edit in three sweeps: particles (does each phrasal verb mean what you think?), mirrors (does each -self word match its subject?), measures (fewer for things you count, less for things you pour).
grammar.practice: Part A — replace the underlined phrase with a phrasal verb from the year: 1) The team departed at dawn. 2) The council promised to investigate the spill. 3) He minimised the damage in his speech. 4) She refused to surrender. Part B — complete with the correct reflexive: 1) Rohan taught ______ to stay calm backstage. 2) We timed ______ during every rehearsal. 3) The founder asked ______ what the bay needed most. Part C — choose the honest quantifier: 1) (Fewer / Less) students missed the deadline this term. 2) There is (a few / a little) time left before the defence. 3) (Most of / Much of) the sources were reliable. Answer key: Part A — 1) The team set off at dawn. 2) The council promised to look into the spill. 3) He played down the damage in his speech. 4) She refused to give up. Part B — 1) himself. 2) ourselves. 3) herself (or himself, matching whichever gender the founder is understood to be — the reflexive only needs to agree with this singular subject). Part C — 1) Fewer students missed the deadline this term (students are countable, so fewer is correct). 2) There is a little time left before the defence (time is uncountable, so a little is correct). 3) Most of the sources were reliable (sources are countable, so most of is correct; much of only fits an uncountable noun).

speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Present four pieces of work from Units 1 to 9 and justify each choice with precise evidence of growth. Name the unit, the skill and the improvement each piece proves. Model line: 'I chose my Unit 4 advert analysis because it shows I can name a persuasive technique and prove its effect on the reader.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to me justify my four portfolio choices and challenge any claim that names no specific evidence.

speaking.title: Comparative reading and interpretation
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Compare two of the five review texts aloud: their purpose, their strongest evidence and their effect on you as a reader. Use at least two fair comparatives and one superlative. Model line: 'Review text 3 argues more patiently than Review text 2, but its evidence about Marka is the most concrete of all five.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to compare two review texts and check my comparatives are fair and my judgements carry evidence.

speaking.title: Research vocabulary in context
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Speak for two minutes about your inquiry topic using at least eight of the thirty review words accurately. A partner ticks each word as it lands and questions any use that sounds forced. Model line: 'My sources were deceptive at first glance, so I had to articulate exactly what each claim was hiding.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Track which review words I use while I describe my inquiry, and quiz me on any I define vaguely.

speaking.title: Six-minute inquiry presentation
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Deliver your full inquiry presentation in five to six minutes: hook, question, evidence from at least three verified sources, conclusion and recommendation. Time yourself, mark two planned pauses, and finish inside the six-minute limit. Model line: 'My question began as a whisper in Unit 1: who benefits if I believe this claim?'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my six-minute presentation, note where I rush or falter, and tell me which section needs rebalancing.

speaking.title: Question-and-answer defence
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Defend your conclusions while a partner asks five challenge questions, at least one about source reliability and one about a counterargument. Answer with evidence, and report your sources fairly: 'The engineer stated that the units had been tested twice.' Model line: 'That is a fair challenge, and my second source answers it directly.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the sceptical examiner for my defence and press me whenever an answer leans on opinion instead of evidence.

speaking.title: Final capstone presentation
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Deliver the polished defence at the capstone exhibition: presentation, questions, then one sentence naming your Grade 9 goal. Stand where everyone can see you, greet your audience, and thank your questioners. Model line: 'Next year I will bring this same evidence discipline to longer essays and faster debates.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Run a final dress rehearsal with me and give last feedback on pace, posture, eye contact and my closing goal.

writing.title: Portfolio evidence annotations
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose four pieces of work from Units 1 to 9 — one reading response, one piece of persuasive or narrative writing, one grammar-rich edit and one recorded speaking task. For each, write one annotation paragraph naming the unit, the skill it proves and the evidence of growth a stranger could verify.
writing.modelText: My Unit 3 letter shows I can make a formal request: I opened with 'It is imperative that', supported it with two counts from the beach survey, and closed with a deadline the council could act on.
writing.sentenceStarter: This piece proves that I can...
writing.expectedLength: Four annotation paragraphs, one per portfolio piece
writing.successCriteria: I named the unit and skill for each piece; I quoted or described verifiable evidence; I explained the growth each piece demonstrates; I kept every annotation concise and specific
writing.support: Use the portfolio checklist and the annotation frame: what it is, what it proves, how it shows growth.
writing.extension: Rank your four pieces from strongest to weakest evidence and defend the ranking in a closing sentence.

writing.title: Inquiry proposal
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write the proposal for your capstone inquiry: the question you will investigate, the defined audience who needs the answer, the three sources you will verify first and the product you will build. Frame the question so evidence could genuinely change your answer.
writing.modelText: My question is: should our school switch to reusable packaging in the canteen? My audience is the school council. My first three sources are the canteen's waste log, the Unit 2 packaging text and an interview with the caterer.
writing.expectedLength: Three focused paragraphs plus a numbered source list
writing.successCriteria: I framed one open, evidence-led question; I defined a real audience; I named three checkable starting sources; I described the final product and its purpose
writing.support: Use the question-storming grid and the audience map from the live session.
writing.extension: Add a fourth paragraph predicting the strongest counterargument your audience will raise.

writing.title: Evidence-led first draft
writing.promptAndInstructions: Draft the full inquiry product: introduction with your question, two or three evidence sections each anchored to an attributed source, and a conclusion that answers the question honestly. Use at least six review words, one passive construction and one reported statement from a source.
writing.modelText: The waste log shows that 340 cups are discarded each week. The caterer stated that reusable cups had been trialled in 2024. If the trial were repeated with deposit tokens, the loss rate would fall.
writing.sentenceStarter: The strongest evidence for my answer is...
writing.expectedLength: Five to seven sustained paragraphs with source evidence
writing.successCriteria: I answered my inquiry question; I attributed every borrowed fact to its source; I used six review words, a deliberate passive and accurate reported speech; I organised sections a reader can follow
writing.support: Use the section planner, the source record and the review-word bank beside you as you draft.
writing.extension: Add a short data table or timeline and refer to it precisely in the text.

writing.title: Substantive revision from feedback
writing.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
writing.promptAndInstructions: Revise your draft using peer and teacher feedback if available, or your AI tutor's feedback if you are working alone. Make at least five substantive changes — reordered sections, strengthened evidence, corrected grammar targets, sharper vocabulary — and keep a change log stating what you changed and why each change improves the product.
writing.modelText: Change 3: I moved the counterargument before my conclusion because the defence questions kept landing there. The section now ends with my strongest source instead of my weakest.
writing.sentenceStarter: The most important change I made was...
writing.expectedLength: The revised draft of five to seven paragraphs plus a five-entry change-log paragraph
writing.successCriteria: I made five or more substantive revisions; I justified each change in the log; I checked comparatives, passives, conditionals and reported speech in a dedicated pass; I kept the strongest feedback and politely declined the weakest
writing.support: Use the revision checklist and the grammar final-edit sweep from workshop six.
writing.extension: Swap logs with a partner and test whether each claimed improvement is visible in the revised draft.

writing.title: Presentation and defence notes
writing.promptAndInstructions: Turn the finished product into speaking notes for the six-minute defence: one paragraph per presentation section, each reduced to a cue line, a key quotation and a timing mark. Then script answers to the three hardest questions you expect.
writing.modelText: Section 2 cue: 'The waste log does not lie.' Quote: 340 cups a week. Time check: two minutes gone. Expected question: how much would tokens cost? Answer: the caterer's trial priced them at forty cents each.
writing.sentenceStarter: If I am asked about my sources, I will say...
writing.expectedLength: One cue paragraph per presentation section, with a question-and-answer paragraph to finish
writing.successCriteria: I reduced each section to a cue, a quotation and a timing mark; I scripted three defensive answers with evidence; I rehearsed from the notes at least once; I kept the total inside six minutes
writing.support: Use the cue-card template and the timing grid from the rehearsal session.
writing.extension: Prepare one honest answer for a question you cannot fully answer yet, naming the evidence you would still need.

writing.title: Grade 8 reflection
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write your Grade 8 reflection: the reader, writer and speaker you were in September, the evidence of who you are now, and one specific, measurable Grade 9 goal. Anchor every claim to a unit, a piece of work or a moment from this year.
writing.modelText: In September I shared claims before checking them. My Unit 1 annotations prove I now ask who benefits first. Next year I will apply the same four questions to the history sources in my Grade 9 essays.
writing.sentenceStarter: The clearest evidence of my growth is...
writing.expectedLength: Four reflective paragraphs and one Grade 9 goal paragraph
writing.successCriteria: I compared my September and June selves with evidence; I named the units and work that prove the change; I set one measurable Grade 9 goal; I wrote honestly about what still needs work
writing.support: Use your portfolio annotations and self-assessment record as memory anchors.
writing.extension: Write a short letter to your September self, warning them about the year's hardest lesson.

activities.title: Curate and annotate evidence
activities.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
activities.instructionsAndItems: Reopen your work from Units 1 to 9 and shortlist eight candidate pieces across reading, writing, grammar and speaking. Test each against three questions: what skill does it prove, what growth does it show, could a stranger verify the claim? Keep the strongest four, one per skill area, and bring them annotated to your first live session if you attend one, or save them as the final piece of evidence in your own portfolio.
activities.answerSummary: Marking guidance and a model shortlist rationale sit in the answer key.

activities.title: Build a research word map
activities.instructionsAndItems: Sort the thirty review words into clusters that match their home units, from communication words such as concise and articulate to judgement words such as benign and deceptive. Add one collocation partner to each word, then star the ten words your inquiry topic will genuinely need and draft one topic sentence using three of them.
activities.answerSummary: Cluster suggestions and collocation examples for checking sit in the answer key.

activities.title: Investigate and verify sources
activities.instructionsAndItems: Apply the Unit 1 fact-checker's toolkit to the three starting sources in your proposal. For each source, record the author, the date, the supporting evidence and who benefits if you believe it, then grade its reliability as strong, usable or weak. Replace any weak source before drafting begins and note what disqualified it.
activities.answerSummary: A worked source-record example and reliability grading notes sit in the answer key.

activities.title: Peer review studio
activities.instructionsAndItems: Exchange drafts with a partner and review theirs against the success criteria: evidence attribution, section order, review-word accuracy and the four grammar targets. Write two precise strengths and one improvement that names a paragraph and a fix. Meet, talk the feedback through, and agree which suggestions each writer will act on.
activities.answerSummary: Feedback sentence frames and a sample completed review sit in the answer key.

activities.title: Rehearse with timing
activities.instructionsAndItems: Rehearse the full defence twice with a visible timer. In round one, mark where you finished each section and where you rushed or faltered. In round two, correct the balance, plant two deliberate pauses and record the run. Listen back once and write down the single change that would most improve round three.
activities.answerSummary: Timing benchmarks and a rehearsal diagnosis guide sit in the answer key.

activities.title: Exhibition and defence
activities.instructionsAndItems: Present at the capstone exhibition: deliver the six-minute defence, answer at least three audience questions with evidence, and collect two pieces of written feedback from listeners. Afterwards, file the product, source record, feedback slips and your reflection in the portfolio and check every checklist item is signed off.
activities.answerSummary: The exhibition marking sheet and completion checklist sit in the answer key.

assignments.title: Grade 8 inquiry capstone and oral defence
assignments.instructions:
Submit the evidence-led inquiry product, attributed source record, four annotated portfolio pieces, six-minute oral defence recording and Grade 9 transition reflection.
Marking guidance for the teacher. Award the 72 marks as follows. Inquiry product, 16 marks: the four writing rubric criteria, four marks each. Oral defence, 16 marks: the four speaking rubric criteria, four marks each, judged on answering for the work rather than presenting it. Attributed source record, 16 marks: 4 for completeness, 4 for accurate attribution, 4 for evaluating reliability, 4 for showing where each source changed the conclusion. Four annotated portfolio pieces, 16 marks: 4 each, awarded for naming the unit, naming the skill and giving a real reason. Reflection, 8 marks: 4 for an honest account of what changed, 4 for a specific and reachable transition goal. Do not award marks for presentation polish or for the materials a family can afford. Assess the English and the reasoning only, and accept scribed or recorded work where a learner needs it.

quizzes.question: Which review word from Unit 1 means 'using few words to say something clearly'?
quizzes.explanation: Concise writing keeps only the words that earn their place, like the questioning club's one-line rule in Unit 1.

quizzes.question: Which sentence compares two climbers correctly?
quizzes.options: Zara climbed more carefully than the lone climber. | Zara climbed most carefully than the lone climber. | Zara climbed more carefully of the lone climber. | Zara climbed the most carefully than the lone climber.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Zara climbed more carefully than the lone climber.
quizzes.explanation: Two actions compared take a comparative adverb with 'than': more carefully than. Superlatives need three or more.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is in the present continuous passive?
quizzes.options: New bins are affixed along the beach paths every season. | Volunteers are affixing new bins along the beach paths. | New bins are being affixed along the beach paths. | New bins will be affixed along the beach paths soon.
quizzes.correctAnswer: New bins are being affixed along the beach paths.
quizzes.explanation: The present continuous passive is are or is plus being plus a past participle, as in Unit 3's clean-up scenes.

quizzes.question: The mayor said, 'The first units will be installed by December.' Which reported version is correct?
quizzes.options: The mayor said that the first units would be installed by December. | The mayor said that the first units will been installed by December. | The mayor said that the first units would being installed by December. | The mayor said that the first units are install by December.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The mayor said that the first units would be installed by December.
quizzes.explanation: Reported speech steps 'will be installed' back to 'would be installed', keeping the passive intact, as practised with Unit 5's story.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the past perfect correctly?
quizzes.options: By morning, a network of writers was form at Kambazi School. | By morning, a network of writers has formed at Kambazi School. | By morning, a network of writers had forming at Kambazi School. | By morning, a network of writers had formed at Kambazi School.
quizzes.correctAnswer: By morning, a network of writers had formed at Kambazi School.
quizzes.explanation: 'By morning' sets a past deadline, so the earlier event takes had plus the past participle: had formed, as in Unit 7.

quizzes.question: Imani ______ her closing story since the opening round of the StoryForge. Which form completes the sentence?
quizzes.options: has been shaping | has shaped being | is been shaping | have been shaping
quizzes.explanation: 'Since the opening round' measures unfinished duration, so the present perfect continuous fits: has been shaping, from Unit 8.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct second conditional?
quizzes.options: If the bay was cleaner, more fish will return. | If the bay were cleaner, more fish would return. | If the bay is cleaner, more fish would return. | If the bay would be cleaner, more fish returned.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If the bay were cleaner, more fish would return.
quizzes.explanation: The second conditional imagines the present: if plus past ('were'), then would plus the base verb, as in Units 3 and 4.

quizzes.question: In 'The officials tried to play down the pollution report', what does 'play down' mean?
quizzes.options: to refuse to talk about something ever again | to make something seem less important | to practise before a serious match | to celebrate a result loudly
quizzes.correctAnswer: to make something seem less important
quizzes.explanation: Play down means to minimise: the officials wanted the report to seem smaller than it was, a phrasal verb from the Unit 7 pattern set.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Review text 3': The park wardens hoped the new signs would ______ visitors from leaving the marked trails.
quizzes.explanation: Review text 3 says the wardens hoped the new signs would deter visitors from leaving the marked trails; deter means to make someone decide not to act.

teacherNotes.note: Conference at each capstone milestone with an adult present, and supervise recorded rehearsals and any online source work directly. Verify responsible attribution and source evaluation at the draft stage, preserve learner ownership of the inquiry question, assess the product and the six-minute oral defence with the shared rubrics, and record specific, actionable Grade 9 transition feedback for every learner.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Strong shortlists pair each piece with a named skill and verifiable growth, for example: Unit 1 comprehension answers beside Unit 7 answers to show inference depth; a Unit 3 formal letter for persuasive register; the workshop-six edit for grammar control; the Unit 9 recording for fluency. Reject any piece whose claim a stranger could not check.

Reference clusters: communication (concise, articulate, clarify, cite-adjacent uses), conflict and power (barricade, usurp, adversary, atrocity), judgement (benign, deceptive, naive, cunning), effort and change (zeal, momentum, wane, falter, aptitude), and time or relief (longevity, reprieve, disposition, commemorate). Accept any defensible cluster; the collocation must be natural, for example 'gain momentum', 'benign smile', 'issue a reprieve'.

A strong source record answers all four toolkit questions with specifics, for example: author named and qualified; dated this year; evidence is a count or document, not an impression; the beneficiary question answered honestly. Grade 'weak' any source with no author, no date or no checkable evidence, and require the learner to name the disqualifying gap.

Model feedback: 'Strength one: every fact in section two is attributed. Strength two: the second conditional in the conclusion matches the evidence. Improvement: paragraph four asserts the trial failed but cites nobody; add the caterer interview or cut the claim.' Reject vague feedback such as 'make it flow better'.

Benchmarks: hook and question inside one minute; evidence sections roughly ninety seconds each; conclusion and recommendation inside the final minute; total between five and six minutes. The diagnosis should name one section to shorten or expand, not a general wish to be faster or calmer.

Score the defence with the speaking rubric across clarity, vocabulary, sentence accuracy and interaction, and the product with the writing rubric. Verify the portfolio holds the product, source record, four annotations, two feedback slips and the reflection before signing the completion checklist.
